title: Teaching is not a vocation. It is a profession.
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes argues that framing teaching as a 'vocation' sounds complimentary but functions as moral exploitation, normalising endless self-sacrifice and making structural workload problems look like tests of personal commitment. Drawing on research into teachers' emotional labour, burnout and attrition (Kinman, Wray and Strange; Madigan and Kim; Ingersoll; Worth and Van den Brande), she argues vocation language is also gendered, since care-coded work is systematically undervalued, and that it distorts workload conversations by making boundary-setting look like a failure of dedication rather than professional self-preservation. Her alternative is 'professional commitment', a framing that holds care and purpose together with expertise, conditions and boundaries. She closes by arguing the 'myth of the born teacher' undermines teacher education, and that teaching should be understood as difficult because it is complex and skilled, not because teachers are expected to suffer.
points: Hughes's central reframe - that 'vocation' language functions as 'moral exploitation dressed up as praise' - directly challenges a widely used and rarely questioned description of teaching.

She cites research (Kinman, Wray & Strange; Madigan & Kim; Ingersoll) linking emotional labour and burnout to attrition, arguing vocation language makes that labour invisible and therefore unprotected.
Her claim that vocation framing is gendered, since feminised, care-coded work is systematically undervalued, connects language choices to structural inequities in how the profession is resourced.
She proposes 'professional commitment' as an alternative frame that holds purpose and boundaries together, arguing teachers who set limits are practising self-preservation, not failing to care.
quotes: But the language of vocation can become dangerous when it is used to imply that because teachers care, they should endure almost anything. This is not professional respect. It is moral exploitation dressed up as praise.
Research on teachers' emotional labour shows that teachers are expected to manage not only what they teach, but how they feel, how they appear to feel, and how they respond to the feelings of others.
If teaching is a calling, then excessive workload becomes a test of commitment rather than a structural problem. The teacher who struggles is not overburdened; they are insufficiently resilient.
A teacher who says, I cannot take on another club, should not be made to feel they have failed children. These are not signs of a weak vocation. They are signs of professional self-preservation.
Let's stop calling teaching a vocation when what we really mean is: do more, give more, absorb more, expect less. Teaching is a profession. And it is time we treated it like one.
